The report highlights the complexity of understanding the supply chains of information systems used by the federal government, as each component may rely on multiple global suppliers. The Software Engineering Institute notes that the identity of these suppliers can be difficult to determine, and federal procurement law and policies promote the use of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) IT products, many of which are manufactured overseas. The Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) requires federal agencies to manage IT security risks, including those related to supply chain vulnerabilities. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has issued guidelines for managing supply chain risk, including due diligence reviews of suppliers and implementing secure configurations. The report also mentions that since 2012, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has issued reports on the risks of the global IT supply chain and made recommendations for improving supply chain risk management. The report concludes by emphasizing the importance of federal agencies addressing the risks of their global IT supply chains as part of their overall IT security programs.

The report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) examines grant programs awarded by the Departments of Health and Human Services (HHS), Labor (DOL), and Justice (DOJ) from 2007 to 2015 that were subject to statutory restrictions on religious-based hiring. The report identified 2,586 grantees who received funding through at least 53 grant programs with such restrictions.

HHS identified one grant program, Projects of National and Regional Significance, administered by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, which allowed primary recipients to be religious organizations and permitted them to hire staff based on their religious beliefs. However, no grants were awarded to these organizations during the study period.

DOL identified 11 grant programs with statutory restrictions on religious-based hiring, but none of the grantees identified were found to have been certified as religious organizations.

DOJ identified 42 grant programs with such restrictions, and nine of the 112 faith-based organizations identified as potential grantees were found to have self-certified as religious organizations.

The report also notes that the agencies did not consistently document or report on grantees' compliance with religious nondiscrimination provisions. The report recommends that the agencies improve their monitoring and reporting on grantees' compliance with religious nondiscrimination provisions.

The report was provided to the Departments of Labor, Justice, and Health and Human Services, as well as appropriate congressional committees, and will be available on the GAO website.
